3.14.1.name: Flaw Remediation
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Find, report and fix system flaws within timeframes you have defined in writing. The assessor checks three things: that you set the timeframes, that flaws are actually identified and reported inside them, and that they are corrected inside them. Patching is the main evidence.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's patch policy says critical and security updates are installed within 14 days of release and everything else within 30, with the MSP's RMM pushing Windows and third-party updates every Wednesday night. The monthly RMM report shows compliance per device, exceptions (the two CNC controllers on a vendor-approved firmware schedule) are documented, and anything that misses the window becomes a ticket.
typical_evidence: Written flaw remediation / patch management policy with defined timeframes
Monthly patch compliance report per device from the RMM or WSUS
Vulnerability scan reports showing findings and their closure dates
Ticket history for exceptions and late patches
Automated check evidence of last update and pending updates (Bulwark checks os.patch.last_update, os.patch.pending_updates)
common_gaps: No written timeframe, so 'timely' cannot be assessed
Servers or CNC controllers excluded from patching with no documented exception
Patches deployed but never verified, so failures go unnoticed
End-of-life operating systems that can no longer be patched
remediation_steps: Write the timeframes down: for example critical within 14 days, others within 30, with named approval for exceptions.
Enable automatic or RMM-managed patching for operating systems and third-party applications.
Produce a monthly compliance report and open tickets for every device that missed the window.
Document vendor-constrained systems (CNC controllers, test equipment) with their own schedule and compensating controls.
Replace or isolate systems whose vendor no longer issues security updates.
Track remaining gaps on the POA&M with dates.

3.14.2.name: Malicious Code Protection
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Anti-malware protection must be running at the places you have designated: endpoints, servers, email and any gateway. Decide where protection belongs, then prove it is there and enabled.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint runs on all 25 PCs and the file server with real-time protection and tamper protection on, managed centrally so users cannot disable it. Email is filtered in the GCC High tenant. The two CNC controllers cannot run an agent, so they sit on a restricted VLAN with no internet access and USB media scanned on a standalone kiosk first, and this is documented as a compensating control.
typical_evidence: List of designated locations for malicious code protection
Central anti-malware console showing every endpoint protected and real-time protection on (Bulwark check os.malware.protection_enabled)
Email filtering configuration
Documented compensating controls for devices that cannot run an agent
Alert history showing detections and responses
common_gaps: Anti-malware installed but real-time protection disabled for performance on CAD machines
No central console, so nobody notices when an agent stops reporting
Shop-floor and legacy systems silently unprotected and undocumented
Free consumer antivirus with no management
remediation_steps: Designate in writing where malicious code protection is required.
Deploy a centrally managed anti-malware product to every endpoint and server and enable tamper protection.
Turn on email and web filtering at the gateway or in the cloud tenant.
For devices that cannot run an agent, document the compensating controls: network isolation, media scanning, allow-listing.
Alert on agents that stop reporting and treat them as incidents.
Review detections monthly.

3.14.3.name: Security Alerts & Advisories
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Monitor security alerts and advisories from credible sources and act on them. Someone must be subscribed, someone must read them, and there must be a record of what you did when one applied to you.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The IT person subscribes to CISA alerts, the Microsoft security update guide and the firewall vendor's advisories, and the MSP forwards anything relevant. Each advisory that applies is logged in a simple register with the date received, affected systems, action taken and date closed. When the firewall vendor published a critical advisory, the register shows the firmware was applied within three days.
typical_evidence: Subscription evidence (CISA, vendor bulletins, ISAC membership)
Advisory register showing received, assessed, action taken and closed dates
Sample advisory with the resulting change ticket
Procedure naming who monitors advisories and how they are dispositioned
Internal notification to staff when user action was required
common_gaps: Alerts delivered to a mailbox nobody reads
No record connecting an advisory to the action taken
Relying entirely on the MSP with nothing in writing about who is responsible
Advisories tracked informally in email threads
remediation_steps: Subscribe to CISA advisories and the vendor bulletins for every product in the boundary.
Name the person responsible for monitoring and a backup.
Keep a simple advisory register with dates and dispositions.
Tie applicable advisories to change tickets so remediation is evidenced.
Define how internal alerts reach staff when user action is needed.
Review the register quarterly.

3.14.4.name: Update Malicious Code Protection
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Anti-malware definitions and engines must be updated whenever new releases are available. This is mostly about proving updates actually land on every device, including ones that are rarely online.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Defender definitions update automatically several times a day; the console flags any device whose signatures are more than three days old, and the weekly report shows all devices current. A CAD laptop that had been off for two weeks showed up in the report, was updated on its return, and the ticket is retained.
typical_evidence: Anti-malware console report showing signature age per device (Bulwark check os.malware.signatures_current)
Configuration showing automatic definition updates enabled
Exception report and remediation tickets for stale devices
Engine version report after a major product update
common_gaps: Laptops that are rarely connected drifting months out of date
Update source blocked by firewall rules for isolated segments
No alerting on stale signatures
remediation_steps: Enable automatic definition and engine updates on every endpoint.
Alert when signatures exceed a defined age, for example three days.
Allow the update source through the firewall for isolated segments or provide an internal distribution point.
Check the console weekly and remediate stale devices.
Record the review so there is evidence it happens.

3.14.5.name: System & File Scanning
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Run periodic scans of your systems and real-time scans of files from external sources as they are downloaded, opened or executed. Define the frequency, then show the scans happen.
guidance.machine_shop_example: A weekly full scan runs Saturday night on every PC and the server, with real-time scanning on for downloads, email attachments and removable media. The console shows the last scan time per device; devices that miss two consecutive scans generate a ticket. USB drives brought in by customers are scanned on a standalone kiosk before use.
typical_evidence: Scan schedule configuration and the defined frequency in policy
Console report of last scan time per device (Bulwark check os.malware.last_scan)
Real-time protection settings covering downloads and removable media
Procedure for scanning incoming removable media
Scan results showing detections and their disposition
common_gaps: Scheduled scans disabled because they slow CAM workstations
Real-time scanning exclusions added broadly, for example the whole jobs folder
No defined frequency in writing
Customer USB drives plugged straight into shop-floor PCs
remediation_steps: Write the scan frequency into policy, for example weekly full plus continuous real-time.
Schedule scans outside production hours and verify they complete.
Review and minimise scan exclusions; document any that remain and why.
Set up a scanning routine or kiosk for incoming removable media.
Alert on devices that miss consecutive scans.

3.14.6.name: Monitor Communications for Attacks
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Monitor the system, including inbound and outbound traffic, to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks. Somebody or something must be watching, and there must be evidence of that watching.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The firewall's IPS is enabled in blocking mode on the internet edge, its logs and the endpoint detection alerts flow to the MSP's monitoring service, and the MSP reviews and triages alerts 24/7 with monthly reports to the owner. Outbound traffic is inspected for known command-and-control destinations, and the monthly report lists what was detected and what was done.
typical_evidence: IPS/IDS configuration on the boundary device
SIEM or managed detection service configuration and coverage list
Monthly monitoring report with alerts and dispositions
Contract or statement of work showing the MSSP's monitoring responsibilities
Endpoint detection and response console showing alert history
common_gaps: Logs collected but no alerting or review
Only inbound traffic watched, with outbound ignored
MSP assumed to be monitoring with nothing in the contract saying so
Alerts going to an unmonitored shared mailbox
remediation_steps: Enable IPS on the boundary firewall and put it in blocking mode after tuning.
Forward firewall, endpoint and server logs to a SIEM or managed detection service.
Define which alerts require action and who responds, including out of hours.
Get monitoring responsibilities written into the MSP or MSSP contract and reflected in the responsibility matrix.
Review the monthly report with the owner and keep it as evidence.
Monitor outbound traffic for command-and-control and data-exfiltration indicators.

3.14.7.name: Identify Unauthorized Use
weight_sources: NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology v1.2.1 Annex A

guidance.summary: Define what authorized use of your system looks like, then be able to spot use that falls outside it: unusual logons, unexpected software, data moving where it should not, accounts doing things they never do.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The acceptable use policy defines authorized use, and the monitoring stack backs it up: alerts fire on logons outside working hours from the shop's accounts, on new admin group membership, on USB mass-storage use, and on large downloads from SharePoint. The IT person reviews the weekly exception report; when an estimator downloaded 400 drawings at 11 pm, the alert triggered a conversation and a documented outcome the same week.
typical_evidence: Acceptable use policy defining authorized use
Alert rules for anomalous logons, privilege changes and large data transfers
Weekly or monthly exception review records
Example investigation with its outcome
Automated check evidence for unauthorised software and accounts (Bulwark checks os.inventory.software, os.accounts.admin_count)
common_gaps: No definition of authorized use, so nothing can be called unauthorized
Alerts configured but never reviewed
No way to see data movement in the cloud tenant
Investigations handled verbally with no record
remediation_steps: Write down what authorized use is, including hours, locations, devices and data handling.
Enable alerting on impossible-travel and off-hours logons, admin group changes and mass downloads.
Turn on unified audit logging in the cloud tenant and retain it.
Review exceptions weekly and record the review and any investigation.
Feed confirmed misuse into the incident response process.
